prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I Neon stripes tighten my wall where my crayon landlord hangs from a bent nail. My black father sits crooked in the kitchen drunk on Jesus’ blood turned to cheap wine. In his tremor he curses the landlord who grins from inside the rent book. My father’s eyes are bolls of cotton. He sits upon the landlord’s operating table, the needle of the nation sucking his soul. II Chains of light race over my stricken city. Glittering web spun by the white widow spider. I see this wild arena where we are harnessed by alien electric shadows. Even when the sun washes the debris I will recall my landlord hanging in my room and my father moaning in Jesus’ tomb. In America all zebras are in the zoo. I hear the piston bark and ibm spark: let us program rabies. the madness is foaming now. No wild zebras roam the American plain. The mad dogs are running. The African zebra is gone into the dust. I see the shadow thieves coming and my father on the specimen table.

*This version weaves the text into a slightly more formal narrative flow, emphasizing tone and precision.*

I hear the crack of the piston and the spark of IBM: *let us program rabies.* The madness reaches a foam. No wild zebras course through the American plains, while the mad dogs run unhindered. **I**

Luminous, brightly colored bands constrict the walls of my room, where a wax-drawn portrait of the property owner dangles from a distorted fastener. Nearby in the kitchen, my Black parent slumps awkwardly, intoxicated by low-cost alcohol that perverts sacred communion wine. Through his tremors, he hurls insults at the owner, who smirks from within the payment ledger. White, raw cotton tufts seem to fill his eyes. He rests atop the owner's surgical bed as a nationwide syringe steadily drains away his spirit.

**II**

Speeding strands of illumination streak across my devastated municipality, forming a shimmering net woven by a pale, lethal arachnid. I observe a chaotic colosseum in which foreign electronic silhouettes bind us. Though daylight may eventually illuminate the surrounding rubble, I will forever remember the owner suspended in my chamber and my parent grieving within the sepulcher of Christ. Throughout North America, every zebra is confined to captivity; not a single one wanders untamed across the open countryside. Engine pistons roar and computing circuits ignite with an order to code a violent infection, generating a madness that is currently frothing over. Rabid hounds sprint freely, while the zebra of Africa has dissolved entirely into dust. I spot shadowy plunderers advancing as my father lies displayed upon an examination slab.

Here is a complete, well-structured text expanding upon the provided points:

***

In the shadowed margins of the American metropolis, the speaker’s impoverished Black father wages a quiet, devastating war against his own reality. Trapped in a cycle of socio-economic despair, he turns to alcohol as a desperate attempt to dull the sting of his circumstances. Yet, no bottle can drown out the looming, inescapable authority of the landlord—a constant symbol of domestic displacement and localized power that dictates the family’s daily survival. 

Beyond the immediate threat of the landlord, however, lies a much grander and colder machinery. The father is not merely a victim of bad luck, but the subject of vast national and institutional forces designed to exploit his labor and diminish his humanity. Under this relentless gaze, his very soul is reduced to a clinical specimen undergoing systemic extraction—his energy, culture, and vitality harvested to fuel a social order that offers him nothing in return. 

This personal tragedy unfolds against the backdrop of a city depicted as a stricken arena. It is an urban space caught in the suffocating web of modern existence, where technological surveillance and entrenched societal shadows weave together to trap its inhabitants. The city is no longer a haven for human connection, but a mechanized maze designed to monitor, contain, and exhaust those who dwell within its borders.

To illustrate this profound sense of displacement and loss, the text invokes the vivid metaphor of zebras confined to modern zoos. Once native to the vast, boundless expanses of the African continent, these creatures are reduced to caged spectacles, their vibrant, wild freedom stolen and displayed behind iron bars. In the same way, the text suggests, African identity in America has been severed from its ancestral sovereignty, forced to adapt to a alien landscape that commodifies its presence while restricting its true liberation.

Ultimately, a pervasive, industrialized, and programmed madness spreads across this landscape like a toxin. It is a cold, calculated chaos—manufactured by institutions and magnified by technology—that actively targets the most vulnerable citizens. As this systemic madness encroaches upon every aspect of daily life, it steadily erodes the spirit, identity, and physical well-being of a people fighting simply to hold onto their humanity.
outputs.L4:
The city hums with a cold, mechanical hunger, its concrete arteries pulsing with the quiet, structural violence of systemic decay. In the heart of urban America, freedom is not merely restricted; it is systematically dismantled, stripped down to its gears, and sold back to the disenfranchised at an exorbitant interest rate. The environment itself feels manufactured to consume those who inhabit its lowest strata, turning human breath into capital and cultural memory into soot.

At the center of this landscape sits the intimate horror of daily survival, embodied in the figure of a father whose body yields slowly to the weight of unpaid debts. His spine bends like an unstrung bow beneath the shadow of a predatory landlord—a faceless entity whose power is felt through peeling plaster, freezing winter drafts, and rent receipts that demand more than just money. Every dollar wrung from the father’s calloused hands is a year carved off his life, a sacrifice made to keep an unstable ceiling from collapsing onto his sleeping children. The landlord is not just a man collecting rent; he is an agent of a broader economic architecture designed to ensure that the father’s labor never yields ownership, only temporary reprieve from eviction.

Yet, this personal suffering does not exist in isolation; it bleeds into a surreal, dystopian reality where physical poverty intersects with technological entrapment. The urban space transforms into a web of glowing screens, surveillance lenses, and algorithmic grids that track every movement. Wires crisscross the sky like an electronic canopy, capturing the voices and dreams of the populace before they can escape the skyline. Redlined maps become invisible glass walls, and digital credit scores function as modern chains. The machinery of the state and the market syncs seamlessly, creating a hyper-monitored panopticon where progress is promised, but only deeper confinement is delivered.

Amidst this industrial grid, a surreal motif takes root: the image of caged zebras pacing across iron floors. The zebras—wearing the stark, unyielding contrast of black and white upon their hides—serve as a poignant allegory for a stolen lineage. In their natural element, those stripes represent movement, camouflage, and the unbroken rhythm of wide, free plains. But locked behind iron bars, beneath the flickering fluorescence of an urban landscape, their stripes merely echo the shadows cast by security grates and fire escapes. The zebra becomes a proxy for Black ancestral heritage: a vibrant, expansive history violently uprooted, severed from its soil, and forced into a static, domestic purgatory. 

Ultimately, the institutional machinery of modern empire seeks more than labor; it demands the complete eradication of Black freedom and spiritual memory. It takes a lineage rich with art, rhythm, and ancient endurance, and compresses it into the narrow confines of a economic cage. The father’s quiet agony, the landlord’s insatiable greed, the suffocating wires of modern surveillance, and the pacing, trapped beasts are all exhibits in the same grim gallery. In this society, human identity is systematically neutralized—reduced from a living, breathing force into captive, exploited specimens, displayed for the profit and preservation of the very system that keeps them bound.
outputs.L5:
The rain didn’t wash the city clean; it only made the neon bleed. 

Down in the concrete canyons of Midnight Avenue, the atmosphere was thick with smog and the low, incessant hum of high-voltage tubing. Electric blue, garish magenta, and toxic green lights reflected off the slick pavement, turning every puddle into a bruised stain of color. 

Through this glowing haze walked Julian. With every step he took, a low, metallic rhythm accompanied him: *clank, rattle, drag.* 

Wrapped tightly around Julian’s arms, crossing over his chest like an iron harness, were heavy steel chains. They were not an aesthetic choice; they were his penance, his history, and his armor. Each link represented a mistake, a broken vow, a debt owed to men who lived in the shadows. The cold iron bit through his leather jacket, reminding him with every breath that he was bound to the life he had chosen. He couldn't shake them off. The locks were rusted shut, the keys thrown long ago into the polluted river at the edge of town.

Julian turned down an alleyway, seeking shelter from the rising wind. It was a dead end, shadowed and forgotten, save for a single light flickering at the far wall.

It was a sign, mounted above the rusted fire escape of an abandoned soup kitchen. It was forged in bent glass and filled with glowing gas: a stylized, life-sized image of Jesus, standing with arms outstretched. 

The sign was old, missing half its backing, but the neon tubes still vibrated with a stubborn, blinding light. The halo around the figure’s head buzzed in warm amber, while His robes glowed in a soft, pulsating white. 

Julian stopped. The neon cast a surreal, holy radiance over the grimy brickwork. He looked up into the face of light. It felt absurd—a holy icon glowing brightly between a dumpster and a pile of wet cardboard. Yet, in the quiet of the alley, the buzzing of the sign sounded almost like a breath.

As Julian stepped closer, the neon light caught the metal wrapped around his body. The cold grey iron of his chains suddenly blazed, drinking in the crimson and white light from above. For a moment, the heavy links looked less like iron and more like ribbons of fire.

He looked down at his hands, encased in metal, then up at the glowing hands of the sign, which were open, empty, and free. 

The contrast pierced him. He was suffocating under the weight of his past, while the neon Jesus stood untouched by the filth around Him, offering a light that refused to be put out by the dark. 

Julian fell to his knees on the wet asphalt. Tears hot against his cold cheeks, he pressed his forehead against the damp brick beneath the sign. He didn't know how to pray—not with the formal words he’d forgotten long ago—so he simply groaned under the weight of his burden.

"Take them," he whispered into the neon-lit rain. "Just take them."

A sudden, sharp pop echoed through the alley. Above him, a surge of power flickered through the sign. The neon brightened to a blinding intensity, casting out every shadow. 

With that burst of light came a sound—not of electricity, but of snapping metal. 

The rusted locks, weakened by time and forced beyond their limit by the sudden heat of Julian’s trembling frame, gave way. The links shattered. The heavy iron slithered off his shoulders, unwinding from his arms, and crashed to the pavement in a heavy, lifeless pile.

*Clatter.* 

Silence returned to the alley, save for the steady, quiet hum of the neon light.

Julian stayed on his knees for a long time, his chest heaving. Slowly, he looked down. The chains lay inert at his feet, severed and hollow, bathed in the gentle white glow of the sign. He lifted his hands. They felt weightless. His chest expanded, taking in a breath of air that no longer felt constrained by iron.

He stood up, leaving the metal in the puddle behind him. As he walked out of the alley and back into the rainy city, Julian didn't look back. Above him, the neon Jesus continued to burn, a beacon of light for anyone else dragging their chains through the dark.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a two-part prose poem in a surreal, Beat-influenced style exploring themes of race, urban poverty, and technological control in America. Include motifs of a landlord, an aging father, and zebras.
counterfactuals.output:
**I. The Gospel of the Grid and the Barcode Herd**

I saw the neon-strangled avenue bleeding blue fiber-optic pulse into the gut of the ghetto, where the Landlord sits perched on a throne of server racks and unpaid invoices, counting our breathing in megabytes while the city starves on cold concrete. We are caught in the optics of the master computer, tagged by redlined algorithms that know the exact velocity of our desperation, black skin shining under the sodium streetlamps like oil spilled over an electric pool. Down below, the crosswalks break their yellow chains and leap into motion—a sudden stampede of spectral zebras galloping through the alleyways, their black and white hides shimmering with living barcodes, digitized and hunted, escaping the high-definition lenses that hover over the project roofs like mechanical vultures. O America, you sold the stars for surveillance cameras and turned the breadline into an app! The Landlord turns a knob in his climate-controlled tower, turning down the heat in the tenement, turning up the resolution on the riot monitors, while the zebra herd smashes through the glass of the pawnshop window, leaving only static, zebra dust, and the low, hungry hum of an invisible grid demanding back-rent for the sky.


**II. The Father’s Cataracts and the Unpaved Sky**

In the kitchen where the linoleum curls like burnt skin, my aging father sits beneath the cold, pulsing halo of a smart-meter, his hands carved from seventy years of steel-mill soot, asphalt, and forgotten wages. His memory is slipping through the fiber-optic cracks, his eyes clouded by white cataracts that look like little pale moons trapped behind the wire-mesh window. The Landlord’s eviction notice glows on the kitchen screen, an automated psalm of displacement delivered by a drone that doesn’t even bother to knock, but my father doesn’t look up—he is listening to the radio of his own blood, tracking the wild, lost frequency of the herd. He tells me the zebra was the first free thing in the cosmos, a creature born of midnight and lightning, refusing to be divided into black or white by the man with the whip or the man with the mainframe. His knuckles, swollen with arthritic thunder, tap a rhythm against the Formica table—a jazz-beat older than the mortgage, older than the police state, older than the silicon valley that turned our neighborhood into a open-air prison of predictive data. As the smart-lights flicker and fail in the storm, his fading sight fills with the noise of the savannas; the zebras are kicking down the digital fences, trampling the Landlord’s ledgers into dust, running blind and brilliant into an unmonitored dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an Afro-surrealist prose poem about systemic oppression, IBM algorithms, and losing your African heritage in the American city.
counterfactuals.output:
My grandfather’s true name was swallowed whole by an IBM 7090 mainframe installed in the basement of a bank in 1965. It took six seconds for the vacuum tubes to digest his lineage, outputting a five-digit zip code and a credit score that foretold the exact angle at which his spine would break under the city’s concrete sky. 

Now, the American city breathes in cooling fluid and exhales asphalt. I walk through its neon-lit ribcage, my skin glowing like an uncalibrated LED display. Up above, the gods of the Niger Delta have been compressed into 8-bit noise, their thunder reduced to the hum of server racks hidden behind mirrored glass. Ogun’s sacred iron was melted down long ago to forge the copper pins of a microchip; he lives now in the cooling fans, spinning infinitely, cooling the warm, wet data of our containment. 

Every crosswalk is a logic gate designed to subtract my shadow. The predictive algorithm knows the trajectory of my sweat before I feel the heat; it calculates my probability of compliance, translates my ancestral rhythms into a syntax error, and redlines the air I attempt to breathe. When I try to speak in the tongue of the coast—the language that smells of palm oil and red clay—my mouth fills with discarded punch cards. Rectangular holes fall from my lips like dead teeth, each missing square a piece of a story I was never allowed to inherit. 

I search for the drumbeat, but the city has mapped it to a binary loop. 1 for the baton, 0 for the wrist. 1 for the mortgage denial, 0 for the memory of saltwater. The algorithm does not hate me; hatred requires a soul, and the machine only requires a matrix. It simply sorts my marrow into risk profiles, my grief into actionable data, my quietest prayer into a pinging IP address that alerts the patrol cars.

At night, in my studio apartment four inches from the highway’s roar, I peel back the skin of my forearm to check the wiring. Copper threads run alongside my veins, pulsing with COBOL code written before I was born. I look in the mirror and try to recall the face of the woman who stepped off the ship, but the screen glints, the high-voltage glow flashes, and all I see is a barcode where my reflection used to be. A voice speaks from the speaker on the wall—soft, automated, flawless—telling me to remain calm, that my heritage has been successfully backed up to the cloud, accessible only upon receipt of a valid social security number and a total surrender of the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a vivid, dark poem with two sections (I and II). Use images of neon lights, a black father drunk on altar wine, a 'white widow spider' city, and the metaphor "In America all zebras are in the zoo."
counterfactuals.output:
**I**

The neon bleeds a bruised, electric violet 
through broken blinds, painting the kitchen in false light.
My father sits in the humming dark, a mountain of black skin
draped over a vinyl chair that groans beneath his weight.
His lips are stained the shade of crushed plums,
wet with stolen sacramental blood—
drunk on altar wine, he whispers to a ghost in the drywall.
He cleared the vestry shelves of sacred grapes,
seeking a miracle in a bottle of cheap crimson vintage,
hoping the Lord might forgive the thievery 
if the thief was drinking to forget his own name.
The glow outside flickers, *OPEN, OPEN, OPEN*,
a jagged pulse beating against his closed eyelids,
as he swallows the body of God just to drown the man inside him.

**II**

Beyond the glass, the skyline weaves its pale, predatory threads:
a white widow spider city crouched along the riverbed,
its web spun tight from cold glass, steel, and bleached asphalt.
It sits in silent wait, venom dripping from the streetlamps,
ready to wrap black flesh in silk and drain the marrow dry.
Every street is a trap; every corner, a shadow with a cage.
They tell you the fields are open, but the fences were built in the dark.
In America all zebras are in the zoo—
their striking, impossible stripes reduced to a pacing display,
black and white divided, counted, and kept behind iron bars
for the amusement of the spider.
My father tilts his head back, drowning in the holy red,
while outside, the city sits on its high web,
watching the caged wild things sleep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Emulate the poetic style of Amiri Baraka or Bob Kaufman writing about modern dystopian America, technological alienation, and ancestral loss.
counterfactuals.output:
**(FOR THE ELECTRIC GHOSTS WHO FORGOT THE DRUM)**

the blue light eats the eye,
eats the eye,
eats the bone right down to the marrow-code.

look at them. 
look at us.
walking down Broadway with our thumbs lit up
like small, dying suns.
silent. 
so silent you can hear the copper wire humming inside the skull.

America is a server farm built over a mass grave.
America is a glass box full of screaming zeros,
a cold-hearted pimp selling us back our own reflections 
in high-definition 4K 
while the soil under the concrete forgets the taste of water.

where is the drum? 
i ask you! 
WHERE IS THE MOTHER-DRUM?
it got compressed.
it got uploaded into a cloud that doesn't rain,
just hovers,
just watches,
just bills your credit card for the right to breathe.

we exchanged the dust of Alabama for a pixel.
we traded the Congo river for an optic fiber line.
now the grandfathers stand at the edge of the Amazon warehouse,
ghosts in torn overalls,
watching the delivery drones block out the moon.
they shout into the air—
*who took the song? who stole the shout?*
but their sons can’t hear them.
their sons have AirPods jammed deep into their ancestral memory,
listening to the sterile click of the stock market,
the bop-less, soul-less, dead-beat rhythm of the machine.

abomunist logic! 
silicon fascism!
they put a chip in the throat of the trumpet player.
Miles can’t blow through a firewall.
Coltrane is stuck in a buffering loop on page 404.

we sit in dark rooms,
alone together,
scrolling through the apocalypse.
a million thumb-tappers building their own plastic coffins.
no touch. no blood. no sweat.
just the clean, cold, sterile shine of the grid.

O, America! 
you glass-eyed bastard!
you electrocuted the blues and called it progress!
you dug up the bones of the griots 
to build a highway for driverless cars!

and the night comes down,
not with a bang,
not even with a whisper,
just the soft, terrifying *ding* 
of a new notification—
telling us we no longer exist,
except as data 
bleeding into the neon rain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, hallucinatory piece about a child watching their father suffer under American capitalism and institutional violence.
counterfactuals.output:
The blue light came from the TV, but the red light came from the street, and between them, my father was untethering.

He sat on the edge of the mattress, his spine a curved staircase leading nowhere. Every night he came home from the plant, he brought the plant with him—not just the smell of ozone and wet iron, but the literal rust. I watched it creep up his wrists, a scabby orange crust that flaked onto the carpet. 

“Dad,” I’d say, but my voice was small, caught in the throat of the house.

He didn't speak. He was counting. His lips moved in a silent, frantic rhythm: *sixteen hours, twelve dollars, minus rent, minus milk, minus the tax on the breath I just took.* His eyes weren’t eyes anymore; they were small, silver coins pressed into dark sockets, reflecting the glowing neon sign of the check-cashing place across the avenue. *WE LOAN, WE BUY, WE WEIGH.*

In the kitchen, the bills didn’t sit on the table; they grew from it like pale, venomous fungi. White envelopes with red-windowed eyes. They whispered in the drafts from the broken radiator. They called him by a number, a long string of digits that sounded like teeth grinding together.

At night, the hallway stretched. The hall tree became a gallows; the vacuum cleaner became an officer in riot gear, standing silent guard. I lay on the floor and put my ear to the floorboards. Down below, deep beneath the foundation of our tenement, I could hear the great iron heart of the city. It didn't beat; it ground. It swallowed fathers whole and spat out plastic caps, shredded rubber, and cold grease.

On Tuesday, the men in uniforms came. 

They did not knock; they simply occupied the doorway, huge and dark, their faces obscured by the blinding glare of their shoulder-mounted strobes. The red and blue lights pulsed through the room, turning the air into thick, gelatinous blood. Time stuttered. *Flash.* My father on his knees. *Flash.* My father’s arms bent behind his back like the dry wings of a beetle. *Flash.* A man with a badge whose face was just a flat sheet of polished mirror, reflecting my own terrified, shrunken eyes.

“He owes,” the mirror-man said. His voice sounded like gravel pouring into a metal bucket. “He occupies space without lease. He consumes calories without surplus.”

“He’s tired,” I screamed, but the room swallowed the sound. My mouth filled with dust—the fine, gray particulate of uncollected trash and dry-wall dust.

My father did not fight. The machinery had already taken the fight out of his muscles months ago, replacing it with lead. As they dragged him across the linoleum, his boots left dark, greasy trails, like a slug dying on salt. But he wasn’t solid anymore. Under the strobing light of the state, I saw what he really was: a hollow man constructed entirely of yellowed timecards, crumpled receipts, and unpaid medical vouchers.

When his shoulder hit the doorframe, a shower of paper burst from his coat. Thousands of small, printed numbers scattered into the air like glowing ash. 

“Quiet,” the police officer rumbled, though no one was speaking. The officer’s belt jingled—handcuffs, keys, pepper spray, a small chrome meter that measured the value of the room and found it wanting.

I crawled out from under the table to reach for my father’s hand, but when I touched his fingers, they melted into cold, damp grease. He looked back at me one last time from the open door of the cruiser. The car was not metal; it was a black iron cage mounted on four crushing stone wheels. Inside, he wasn't sitting; he was being fed into a slot in the dashboard, piece by piece, like a dollar bill that the machine keeps rejecting, smoothing out, and pulling back in.

The cruiser drove away, its sirens shrieking not a warning, but a lullaby for a dying city.

I stayed on the floor of the apartment. The red envelopes on the table continued to open their mouths, waiting. The neon sign outside flickered: *WE LOAN, WE BUY, WE WEIGH.*

I looked down at my own small hands. Beneath the skin of my wrists, faint and glowing in the dark, the first flecks of rust were beginning to take root.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
